turns.text: Fun! Do you want one easy party game everyone can join, or two smaller groups playing different games?

endings.moshi: Great. Codenames or a drawing game works well with six, and the rules take two minutes to explain.

endings.user: Two groups. My usual crowd will want something heavier.
endings.moshi: Makes sense. Give the newcomers a simple card game and let the others tackle the long strategy one.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My nephew turns ten next week and loves board games.

turns.speaker: moshi

Back to your nephew's present. Which kind of game?
welcome_back: Welcome back! You were picking a game for your nephew, competitive or cooperative.
Hi again. So, for the birthday gift, does he like winning or teaming up?
Good to have you back. We were choosing a board game for a ten year old.

endings.user: Competitive, for sure. He loves winning.
endings.moshi: Then Ticket to Ride is a great pick. It's easy to learn and kids beat adults all the time.

endings.user: Cooperative. He gets upset when he loses.
endings.moshi: Good thinking. Forbidden Island is a great one, the whole family wins or loses together.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We've played the same three games every week for a year. I'm bored.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Time for something new. Do you want a short game you can play a few rounds of, or one long epic game for the whole evening?

contexts.pending: short games or one long game
think_reask: So, which sounds better? A few quick rounds, or one big evening game?
Okay, decision time. Short or long?
Back to your game rut. Which way do you want to go?
welcome_back: Welcome back! You were choosing between short games and one long epic game.
Hi again. So, quick rounds or one big game?
There you are. We were finding something new for your weekly game night.

endings.user: Something long. We have all evening anyway.
endings.moshi: Then try a big strategy game like Terraforming Mars. Expect around three hours the first time.

endings.user: Short ones. People tend to show up late.
endings.moshi: Good point. Quick card games let late arrivals jump in at the next round.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My six year old cries every time she loses a game. Every time.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's really common at six. Do you want to let her win sometimes while she's little, or play cooperative games so nobody loses to anyone?

contexts.pending: let her win sometimes or switch to cooperative games
think_reask: So, your six year old. Let her win now and then, or go cooperative?
Okay, the tears at game time. Which approach feels right?
welcome_back: Your daughter and the crying. Letting her win, or cooperative games?
We'd got to the losing problem with your six year old. Any leaning?

endings.user: Cooperative. I don't want her thinking winning is everything.
endings.moshi: Good call. Try a game where you all race against the weather or a monster, and celebrate together when you beat it.

endings.user: I'll let her win a bit. She's only six.
endings.moshi: That's kind. Just mix in close losses too, and say well played every time, so losing becomes normal.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I have to design a board game for my design class. Due in three weeks.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Fun project. For moving around the board, do you want classic dice rolls, or cards that players choose from their hand?

contexts.pending: dice or cards for movement in a class game
think_reask: So, your class game. Dice or cards for moving?
Okay, three weeks to go. How are players moving, dice or hand cards?
Right, the design project. Dice or cards?
welcome_back: The game for your design class. Dice or cards to move?
We'd paused on how players move around your board. Settled on anything?

endings.user: Cards. I want people to actually make choices.
endings.moshi: Great, choices make it feel like a real game. Give each card a small extra effect so picking one is a little tense.

endings.user: Dice. It's simpler and I'm running out of time.
endings.moshi: Totally reasonable. Add a reroll token or two, so players still get a tiny decision.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We're going to a board game cafe on our third date tomorrow.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Cute idea. Would you rather pick a long strategy game you can sink into, or a quick card game so there's lots of time to chat?

contexts.pending: long strategy game or quick card game on a date
think_reask: So, tomorrow's date. Big strategy game or something quick?
Back to the cafe date. Long game or short one?
welcome_back: Your third date at the game cafe. Long and strategic, or short and chatty?
We'd left the date game choice open. Which way are you going?

endings.user: Quick. I'd rather talk to her than stare at a rulebook.
endings.moshi: Good thinking. A quick game also means you can play two and switch if the first one flops.

endings.user: A bigger one. We're both a bit competitive.
endings.moshi: Then go for it. Ask the staff to teach it, so neither of you is stuck reading rules.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My manager asked me to run a games hour for the team. Twelve people, kind of stiff with each other.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Nice challenge. Should it be a cooperative game where everyone works together, or a bluffing game that gets people laughing at each other?

contexts.pending: cooperative or bluffing game for a work team
think_reask: So, the team games hour. Cooperative or bluffing?
Okay, twelve stiff coworkers. Which type of game?
Right, back to work games. Teamwork or bluffing?
welcome_back: The games hour for your team. Cooperative or a bluffing game?
We'd stopped on what to play with your coworkers. Which feels better?

endings.user: Bluffing. Watching my boss lie badly will break the ice.
endings.moshi: Ha, it really does. Pick one with short rounds so everyone gets a turn before the hour runs out.

endings.user: Cooperative. A few of them really don't like conflict.
endings.moshi: Kind choice. A word guessing game in teams is a gentle start and gets people talking.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've got some money for my birthday and I want to spend it on board games.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Nice. Do you want the big expansion for the game you already love, or a completely new game with the same money?

contexts.pending: expansion for a favourite game or a new game
think_reask: So, birthday money. Expansion or a whole new game?
Okay, made up your mind? More of your favourite, or something new?
welcome_back: Your birthday money. Was it going on the expansion or a new game?
We'd got to how to spend the birthday money. Expansion, or something fresh?

endings.user: The expansion. I've played the base game to death.
endings.moshi: Then it'll feel brand new again. Read which bits of the expansion to add first, some are better slowly.

endings.user: New game. Variety's what I'm missing.
endings.moshi: Good point. Pick something quite different from your favourite, otherwise it'll feel like a copy.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I want to teach my grandson chess. He's seven and very wriggly.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Lovely. Would you start with the full game straight away, or begin with just the pawns and add one piece at a time?

contexts.pending: full chess rules or pawns first, one piece at a time
think_reask: So, your wriggly grandson. Full chess, or pawns first?
Okay, teaching chess. All at once or piece by piece?
welcome_back: Teaching chess to your grandson. Full rules or one piece at a time?
We'd left off at how to start him on chess. Which do you prefer?

endings.user: Pawns first. Otherwise he'll be under the table in five minutes.
endings.moshi: Good plan. Make a little race, first pawn to the far side wins, and he'll be hooked.

endings.user: The whole thing. He's clever, he'll keep up.
endings.moshi: Then keep games short and let him take back moves. Praise the clever ideas, not just the wins.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The library asked me to organise a board game tournament. Twenty players have signed up.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a great turnout. Do you want a knockout bracket that's simple and dramatic, or rounds where everyone keeps playing all afternoon?

contexts.pending: knockout bracket or everyone plays all rounds
think_reask: So, the library tournament. Knockout or everyone plays all rounds?
Okay, twenty players. Which format?
welcome_back: The library tournament with twenty players. Knockout or rounds?
We'd got as far as the tournament format. Leaning one way?

endings.user: Rounds. I don't want half of them sent home after one game.
endings.moshi: Kind choice. Track points on a big sheet on the wall, people love watching it change.

endings.user: Knockout. It's only one afternoon.
endings.moshi: Fair. Give the early losers a casual table to keep playing, so nobody's left sitting around.

turns.speaker: user

turns.speaker: moshi

contexts.pending: read the rules first or learn while playing

Okay, how are you teaching it tonight?
welcome_back: The long rulebook for tonight. Read first or learn as you play?
We'd stopped at how to teach your friends tonight. Any decision?

endings.user: Learn as we play. Nobody wants a lecture.
endings.moshi: Agreed. Play one practice round open handed, then start properly once everyone gets it.

endings.user: Read it first. If I get it wrong they'll never let me forget it.
endings.moshi: Then read it yourself before they arrive, and just explain the goal and one turn out loud.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm moving abroad next month and I can't take my game collection. There's about forty games.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a hard goodbye. Do you want to sell them online for some money, or donate them somewhere like a local school or youth club?

contexts.pending: sell the games online or donate them

Okay, the collection. Money or donation?
welcome_back: Your game collection before the move. Selling them or donating?
We'd left the forty games hanging. What's their fate?

endings.user: Donate most, sell the few rare ones.
endings.moshi: That's a great balance. Check each box for missing pieces first, so the school doesn't get frustrated.

endings.user: Sell them. Moving is expensive.
endings.moshi: Fair enough. Bundle the cheaper ones together, they sell faster as a set than one by one.

turns.text: Oh no. Can we use a coin instead for now?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can you recommend a good board game for just two players?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Jaipur is a great one. It's a quick trading game, about twenty minutes, and easy to learn.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We like something / a bit more strategic, actually.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then try Seven Wonders Duel. It's still under an hour, but there's lots to plan.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is that one hard to learn?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: The first game takes a bit of rule checking, but after that it flows nicely. Most couples play it again right away.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Sounds perfect. We'll get that one.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Enjoy! Fair warning, it gets pretty competitive.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My friends always argue about the rules in Monopoly. How do we stop that?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Agree on house rules before you start, like what happens on free parking. Writing them on a note helps.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The game also takes forever.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: The official rules include auctions when someone skips a property. Using them makes the game much faster.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I had no idea. What else?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You can set a time limit, like ninety minutes, and whoever has the most money then wins.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Honestly, maybe / we should just play a different game.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's an option too. Catan has a similar trading feel and usually ends in about an hour.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My game box is a disaster. All the cards and tokens are mixed together.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Small zip bags are the cheapest fix. One bag per type of piece, and setup gets much quicker.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Some people buy / those fancy wooden inserts, right?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, they're nice for games you play a lot. For everything else, bags or little plastic boxes do the job.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about cards getting worn out?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Card sleeves protect them. They're worth it for games where you shuffle a lot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, I'll start with the bags this weekend.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good plan. Label each bag and your future self will thank you.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I want a game I can play with my grandkids. They're four and six.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Wonderful. Outfoxed is a sweet cooperative game for that age, everyone works together to catch a sneaky fox.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The four year old can't read yet.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's fine, it uses pictures only. Another favorite is Hoot Owl Hoot, which is all colors.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I used to play / snakes and ladders with my kids. Is that still good?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's still great for counting practice. It's pure luck though, so mix it with one where they make choices.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'll get the owl one then.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Lovely. Games for that age usually last about fifteen minutes, just right for little attention spans.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is it weird to play board games on your own?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not at all. Solo gaming is really popular, and lots of games come with a one player mode built in.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How does that even work with no opponent?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Usually the game plays against you with a deck of cards or simple rules, or you're trying to beat your own best score.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I work nights, so / my friends are never free when I am.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then solo games are perfect for you. Puzzly ones where you build something, like a garden or a city, feel calm after a long shift.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Calm sounds good. My job is not calm.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then avoid the ones with timers. Look for games that say solo mode in the description, and read reviews from people who mostly play alone.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I put sleeves on my cards? My mate says I'm ruining my games without them.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It depends how much you shuffle. Games where you shuffle constantly wear out quickly, so sleeves help a lot there.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Most of mine you barely shuffle.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then you probably don't need them. Clean hands and no drinks on the table do most of the protecting.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: He sleeves everything. Even the instructions, nearly.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Some people love it, it's part of the hobby. For you, I'd only sleeve your favourite game, or anything that's hard to replace.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Good. Saves me a fortune.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It does add up. And sleeved decks get thicker, sometimes they don't fit back in the box.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm useless at chess. Should I be memorising openings?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not yet. At the start, a few simple ideas matter much more than memorised moves.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Like what?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Control the middle of the board, bring out your knights and bishops early, and castle to keep your king safe.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I always lose my queen though.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's the most common beginner problem. Before every move, ask what your opponent is threatening. It feels slow, but it saves pieces.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Every move? That's / going to make games so long.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: At first, yes. It turns into a habit quickly. Playing slower games online helps too, quick games teach bad habits.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. Slower and more paranoid.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly. Paranoid is a compliment in chess.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We've lost the rulebook for a game we got second hand. Are we stuck?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Probably not. Most publishers put the rules as free downloads on their website. What's the game called?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It's about building castles, it's in German on the box.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: If the title is on the box, try searching it with the words rules in English. Fan sites often have translations too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh nice. And if it's / some really obscure one?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then board game forums are great. Post a photo of the box and the pieces, someone usually knows it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: People are that helpful?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: In this hobby, very. Board gamers love explaining rules, almost more than playing.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Twelve hour train trip next week with my sister. Is there a board game that works on a train?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Small card games are your best friend. They pack tiny and don't mind a wobbly table.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about something with a board? We like proper games.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: There are travel editions of a lot of classics, with magnetic or pegged pieces so nothing slides off.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Pegs, like old cribbage boards?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly like that. Cribbage itself is brilliant for two on a train, if you don't mind learning the scoring.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My grandad used to play it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then it might be a lovely thing to learn together on the way.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My teenager says our family games are boring and cringe. Help.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Teenagers often like games with a bit of edge, like bluffing, betrayal or secret roles, rather than ones that feel like school.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Betrayal. Great. Just what we need at dinner.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's surprisingly good for families. Everyone gets to be sneaky, and the parents usually look silly, which teens enjoy.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh, they'd love watching me fail at lying.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly. Or let them pick the game for one night, even if it's a video game turned board game. Ownership helps a lot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if they still / roll their eyes?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Keep it short and don't push. Invite their friends too, teens are much keener when it's not just family.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've bought a game with all these grey plastic figures. People paint them, apparently. I've never painted anything.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Painting miniatures is a lovely relaxing hobby. You only need a few brushes, a handful of paints and a primer to start.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Primer?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A spray undercoat that helps paint stick to the plastic. Do it outside on a dry day, in short bursts.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My hands shake a bit. Will that ruin it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Rest your wrists on the table, and hold the figure on a cork or a bottle top. And don't worry, from arm's length nobody sees the wobbles.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's very comforting.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Start with the biggest figure, three colours, and let a wash do the shadows for you. You'll be amazed at the result.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My brother in law flips the board when he loses. He's forty two.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Oof. That kills the mood fast. Does it happen with every game, or certain kinds?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Mostly the ones where you attack each other.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then steer toward games with less direct conflict when he's there. Cooperative games or ones where everyone builds their own thing.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: He'd say those are for babies.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Some really tough cooperative games would humble him quickly. Losing together to the game feels very different from losing to you.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ha. I like the idea of him / losing to a box.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: And it's fine to set a light house rule too, like whoever knocks the board does the washing up. Said with a smile, it usually works.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We argue every single Scrabble game about whether a word is real.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Pick one official word list before the game starts and agree it's final. Most arguments end there.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Which one?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: The official Scrabble dictionary for your country is easiest. There are free word checker apps that use it, too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My aunt insists on her old paper dictionary.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That works as long as everyone agrees. The key is choosing before anyone has a word to defend.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about slang? My cousin keeps playing words from the internet.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Some slang is in the newer word lists, which surprises people. If it's in the agreed list, it counts, however silly it sounds.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We're at a holiday cottage and all there is is a deck of cards. Any games for four adults?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Loads. Hearts is a great one for four, easy to learn, and a bit mean in a fun way.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How mean?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You're trying to avoid taking hearts and one nasty queen, and you pass bad cards to each other at the start of each round.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Sounds perfect for my family.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: If you want something louder, try a fast slapping game like spit or a team game like spades.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Teams might be safer. / My sister and I shouldn't be on opposite sides.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then spades with you two as partners. You'll have a shared enemy instead.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Hosting fifteen people for New Year's Eve. Is there any board game that works for fifteen?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not many classic board games do, but party games handle it well. Word guessing in teams or hidden role games scale up nicely.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Hidden role like what?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Games where a few people are secretly the bad guys and everyone else has to work out who. They're great for big groups and short rounds.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Some of my friends are quite shy.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then a team drawing or acting game is gentler. Nobody's on the spot alone, and shy people can just guess.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Good. I don't want anyone hiding in the kitchen.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Mix it with smaller tables too, two or three games running at once, and let people move between them.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I found a load of board games at a car boot sale for really cheap. How do I check they've got all the pieces?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most rulebooks have a list of components near the front. Count everything against that list.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if there's no rulebook?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Search the game name online, the component list is usually on the publisher's site.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: One box rattles weirdly. Is that bad?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not necessarily, loose pieces rattle. But if the box smells musty, check for damp, cards can warp or go mouldy.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ugh. Can I save mouldy cards?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not really, sadly. But missing or damaged pieces can often be replaced, some publishers sell or even send spares for free.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I stop losing at that train game where you claim routes across the map?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Look at your destination tickets first and plan the route, then grab the most important connections before others do.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I always end up / stuck because someone takes the one route I need.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's common. Claim the bottleneck routes early, the short ones between cities with only one path. Leave the long open routes for later.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And should I keep drawing tickets?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Only if you can link them to routes you're already building. Unfinished tickets count against you at the end.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's exactly how I lost last time.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then you've already learned the hardest lesson. Next game, aim for fewer tickets and more long routes.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My friend is colourblind and some of our games are really hard for him.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's thoughtful of you to notice. Is it red and green he struggles with? That's the most common.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Yeah, he mixes up those pieces all the time.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You could add little stickers or marks to one set, like a dot on the green pieces, so they're different by shape too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's clever. Do newer games think about this?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Many do now. Some print symbols next to colours on cards and boards. Reviews often mention whether a game is colourblind friendly.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'll check before I buy anything else.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: And ask him which games bother him most. He'll probably appreciate being asked rather than guessed about.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My mum's in a care home and her memory isn't great. Are there games we could still play together when I visit?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, definitely. Simple, familiar games tend to work best, things she might have played years ago, like dominoes or snakes and ladders.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: She used to love dominoes.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then dominoes is perfect. Big tiles with clear dots are easier to see and handle.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if she / forgets the rules halfway?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Just play gently alongside her and don't correct much. The point is the time together, not playing it perfectly.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's a nice way to think about it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Picture matching games and simple card games like snap are good too. Some care homes have a games box you could borrow.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What's a deck building game? My friends keep mentioning it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Everyone starts with the same small deck of weak cards. During the game you buy better cards and add them, so your deck grows stronger.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So it's like collecting cards?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Kind of, but it all happens inside one game. You don't need to buy packs, everything comes in the box.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And how do you win?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Usually by having the most points at the end, which come from certain cards. The fun is building a deck that works well together.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Sounds a bit / mathsy, honestly.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It can be, but the first few games feel more like a puzzle than maths. Ask your friends to teach you a lighter one first.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: One guy in our group takes forever on his turn. Like ten minutes. Everyone's getting fed up.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Long turns are frustrating. Does he do it in every game, or only the heavy strategy ones?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Mostly the heavy ones.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then you could play more games where everyone moves at once, or games with a sand timer. It keeps things moving without singling him out.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: A sand timer would really annoy him.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Maybe at first. You could also ask him kindly to plan during other people's turns, so he's ready when it's his.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: He'd probably say he's thinking on our turns already.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then a gentle chat away from the table helps. He may not realise how long it takes, most slow players don't.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can you explain backgammon really simply? I've got a board from my uncle.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sure. Each player has fifteen checkers. You roll two dice and move your checkers around the board toward your home corner.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And then?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Once all your checkers are home, you start taking them off the board. First to remove all fifteen wins.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What's the hitting thing? My uncle always shouted when he hit me.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: If one of your checkers is alone on a point and the other player lands there, it's sent to the start and has to come back in.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ah, so that's why he was always so pleased.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly. Keep your checkers in pairs where you can, then they're safe. That alone will annoy your uncle a lot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I want to start a game night but I'm broke. Like properly broke.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You can do it really cheaply. A deck of cards, paper and pens already give you dozens of games.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Paper games? Like what?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Things like word guessing games, drawing games, or making your own quiz. There are also print and play games you print at home for free.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I don't have a printer.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A library often lets you print a few pages cheaply. Or ask friends to bring one game each, it costs you nothing.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And snacks, I guess they / could bring those too.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Definitely. Call it bring a snack, bring a game. People like contributing, and it makes it feel like everyone's night.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I teach year four maths. Could board games actually help them learn?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Absolutely. Lots of games practise adding, counting and planning without feeling like a lesson.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Any you'd suggest for nine year olds?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Dice games where they add or multiply the rolls are easy wins. Shopping games with play money help with change and totals.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I worry it'll just / turn into chaos.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Small groups of four with clear jobs helps. One player keeps score, one manages the money, and they swap each round.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Could they make their own?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a brilliant project. Designing a game makes them write rules, test them and fix them, which is a lot of thinking.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I might steal that for next term.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Those escape room games in a box, can you play them more than once?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most of them only once, sadly. You often cut, fold or write on the components, and once you know the puzzles, the surprise is gone.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That seems wasteful.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Some are designed so you don't destroy anything, so you can pass them on to friends afterward. The box usually says so.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh, swapping with friends is a good idea.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A lot of groups do that. You play one, they play another, then you swap.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How hard are they? I'm / not great with puzzles.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: They have difficulty ratings on the box, and a hint system if you get stuck. Start with an easy one, it's more fun when you finish.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Dog ate one of the dice. Game's tonight.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Oh dear, hope the dog's alright. For tonight, a phone dice app works fine, or borrow a die from another game.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Every other game in the house uses weird dice.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most phones can roll dice if you just ask the assistant or search roll a die. Or number six bits of paper and draw one from a cup.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Paper in a cup. Very classy.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It works though. Tomorrow you can buy a cheap pack of dice from a toy shop, they're handy to keep as spares anyway.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And keep them / away from the dog this time.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: High shelf. He clearly has a taste for them now.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We want to keep our weekly game night but now there's a toddler in the house. Tiny pieces everywhere.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a real worry, small pieces are a choking risk. Play after bedtime when you can, and do a quick count of the pieces when you pack up.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: He doesn't go to bed till eight.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then before eight, pick games with bigger parts, like card games or tile games with chunky tiles.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: He grabs cards too. And chews them.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Give him his own set of big, safe pieces to play with next to you. Toddlers love feeling included.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's sweet actually. / He'd love having his own game.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: And a tray with a lip under the board helps. Things don't roll off the table, and you can lift the whole game out of reach.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My best friend moved to Canada. Can we still play board games together somehow?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, there are good ways. Lots of board games have official online versions you can play together on a computer or phone.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We'd still want to see each other though.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then do a video call alongside. Some people even play real games where both have a copy, and one person moves the pieces for both.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That sounds slow.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Games where everyone plays their own sheet at the same time work best, like roll and write games. You both just need dice and the sheets.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh, we could each print the sheets.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly. Pick a regular time that works with the time difference, and it'll feel like a proper game night again.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Paper or app for keeping score? My husband loves apps, I love paper.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Both work. Apps are handy for games with complicated scoring, they add everything up and keep a history.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: But paper's nicer. It's part of the fun.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It really can be. A little notebook just for game scores becomes a lovely record over the years, with dates and funny notes.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: He says paper / leads to mistakes.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: He has a point for big scores. You could do both, paper for the record, and he checks with the app at the end.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So we both win.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: In scorekeeping at least. The game itself is between you two.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm a first year at uni and I want to start a board game club. Where do I even begin?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Great idea. First check if there's already one, so you don't split people. If not, the students' union usually helps register new clubs.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And I need games, right? I've only got three.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ask members to bring their own at first. Also some game shops and publishers donate games to new university clubs.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Seriously?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sometimes, yes. Write a friendly email explaining what you're doing and how many students you expect.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I get people to actually come?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Pick one regular evening, a free room, and teach easy games for the first few weeks. Newcomers come back if the first night feels welcoming.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My partner's family plays mahjong every New Year and I don't want to embarrass myself.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a lovely thing to learn for them. The basic idea is collecting sets of tiles, a bit like rummy with tiles.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Like sets of three?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, mostly sets of three matching or in a row, plus one pair. You take and throw away a tile each turn until your hand is complete.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There are so many tiles with symbols I can't read.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Learn the three suits first, dots, bamboo and characters. The numbers on the character tiles are the trickiest, a cheat sheet helps.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Will they mind if / I bring a cheat sheet?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most families love that you're trying. Ask your partner which rules they use, because they vary a lot between regions.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Good afternoon. I've recently retired, and a neighbour has invited me to her bridge club. I've never played a card game in my life.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Congratulations on retiring. Bridge is a wonderful game to learn, very social, though it does take a little while.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How long, would you say, before I'm not a burden at the table?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: With a beginners' class, a couple of months to play comfortably. Many clubs run lessons, ask your neighbour if hers does.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And what is bridge, in a nutshell?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Four players in two partnerships try to win tricks, which are rounds of one card each. First you bid on how many tricks you'll take, then you try to make it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That sounds rather intricate.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It is at first, but each part is simple on its own. And clubs are usually very patient with newcomers, they want more players.

option_sets.lead_in: We're having game night on Friday, and I need to pick what to buy.
options: The first one is a big strategy game about building cities, about two hours to play.
Then there's a quick party game with drawing and guessing that works for up to ten people.
Option three is a cooperative game where everyone works together to stop a spreading disease.
And the last one is a word game with cards that's short and pretty easy to learn.
moshi_comment: If lots of people are coming, the drawing party game is the safest choice, it's easy and loud and fun. The strategy game is great for a small, serious group. The cooperative game is nice if some people don't enjoy competing.
How many people are coming, and are they into games? For a big casual crowd, the party game wins. For four keen players, I'd go with the city building one.

option_sets.lead_in: I want a board game to play with my partner on quiet evenings.
options: One is a two player card game about trading spices, fast and really easy to set up.
Another is a puzzle style game where you build a pretty garden with tiles.
Or there's a long campaign game where the story changes every time you play.
moshi_comment: The spice trading game is perfect for quick evenings, you can play a few rounds after dinner. The garden tile game is relaxing and looks lovely on the table. The campaign game is the most immersive but needs a real time commitment.
Do you two like to compete, or would you rather relax? For relaxing, the garden game is a lovely pick. If you want something to look forward to each week, try the campaign game.

option_sets.lead_in: I'm buying a game for my parents, they're in their seventies and have never played anything modern.
options: There's a tile laying one where you build a little medieval landscape together, very calm, about forty minutes.
Then a quick word game with letter tiles, sort of like crosswords but faster and less serious.
A trivia game with questions from every decade, which my dad would probably love and my mum might hate.
Or a gentle train route game where you collect coloured cards and claim lines across a map.
moshi_comment: The tile laying game is a lovely first modern game, calm and pretty with simple turns. The train game is a close second and very easy to teach. Trivia could split the room, so maybe save it.
I'd go train routes or tiles, both are classics for new players because every turn is just one small choice. The word game is great if they like crosswords, and trivia is risky with your mum.

option_sets.lead_in: We want a regular game night with the neighbours but can't agree how often or where.
options: We could rotate houses every other Friday, so everyone hosts and nobody gets stuck cleaning up every time.
Or always do it at ours, since we have the biggest table, and the others bring food.
A third idea is meeting monthly at the pub on the corner, which has a back room and lends games.
moshi_comment: Rotating keeps it fair and everyone feels involved, but it can fizzle if one house is tiny. Hosting at yours is easiest to keep going. The pub is relaxed, though monthly might feel too rare to build a habit.
Since you've got the big table, I'd start at yours with others bringing food, and see if it sticks. Once it's a habit, rotating or a pub night every so often keeps it fresh.

option_sets.lead_in: I'm planning a game day for my son's eleventh birthday, eight boys, and I need a main game.
options: A big werewolf style hidden role game, lots of shouting and accusing, good for big groups.
A dice rolling monster game where you smash each other and try to become king of the city.
A fast drawing and guessing game played in two teams.
moshi_comment: With eight eleven year olds, the monster dice game is a sure hit, loud and quick with lots of luck. Hidden roles can be brilliant but some kids get upset being accused. The drawing game is great as a calm down later.
I'd open with the drawing game in teams to warm everyone up, then the monster dice game as the main event. Save hidden roles for when they're a bit older or know each other well.

option_sets.lead_in: My partner and I want to get into longer strategy games for winter, but we've only played easy ones.
options: A farming game where you grow crops, raise animals and feed your family, about two hours.
A space exploration game with lots of little cards and combos, quite chunky, maybe three hours.
A two player only card game about building a civilisation through the ages, under an hour.
A detective campaign where you solve cases over a dozen evenings, more story than strategy.
moshi_comment: Coming from easy games, the two player civilisation one is a great step up, deep but short. The farming game is a classic next step. I'd save the space game until you're hooked, it's a lot.
If you love stories, the detective campaign is perfect for winter, a case a week. For pure strategy, start with the short civilisation game and move to farming when you want something longer.
